la:noun:tyrannus.html:
tўrannus, i, m., = τύραννος.
In gen., a monarch, ruler, sovereign, king (rare, and mostly poet.): tyrannusque fuerat appellatus (Miltiades), sed justus ... omnes autem et dicuntur et habentur tyranni, qui potestate sunt perpetuā in eā civitate, quae libertate usa est,; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Of the Spartan king Nabis, .—Of Neptune, .—Of Pluto, .—Of the constellation Capricornus, because it ruled over, influenced the ocean, Hor C. 2, 17, 19.—
In partic., a cruel or severe ruler, a despot, tyrant: tyrannorum vita,; ; : importunus atque amens,; ; : cum exitiabilis tyrannus (urbem) vi atque armis oppressit,: tyrannorum ingeniis mors est remedium,; ; ; ; : animus noster modo rex est. modo tyrannus; ubi impotens, cupidus, delicatus est, transit in nomen detestabile ac dirum, et fit tyrannus,.—Gen. plur.: tyrannūm novi temeritudinem, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 79 Rib.: non tyrannum novi, as acc. sing.).

la:noun:tyrannis.html:
tўrannis, ĭdis (acc. tyrannida, ), f., = τυραννίς.
The sway of a tyrant, arbitrary or despotic rule, tyranny: o di boni! vivit tyrannis, tyrannus occidit,; cf.: sublato tyranno tyrannida manere video,: tyrannidem occupare,; so : affectare,; : delere,: destruere,; ; ; , ext. 1; 8, 9, ext. 2: (Pythagoras) odio tyrannidis exsul Sponte erat,: tyrannis saeva crudaque Neronis,.—
Transf., the region ruled by a tyrant: quinque et viginti talenta tyrannidem tuam exhaurirent?.—
A female tyrant, Treb. XXX. Tyr. 31 fin.; cf. tyranna.

Lit.
Esp., as beaten by the priests of Cybele, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; , 105; ; ; , —Also by the Bacchantine females, .—Beaten by the Parthians as a signal in battle in place of the tuba, .—
Trop., a timbrel, etc., as a figure of something effeminate, enervating: tympana eloquentiae,: in manu tympanum est,.—
Transf., of things of a like shape.
A drum or wheel, in machines for raising weights, in water-organs, etc., ; ; ; ; .—
In archit.
The triangular area of a pediment, —
A panel of a door, —
A part of the clepsydra, called also phellos, .

la:noun:Tyrus.html:
Tўrus or -ŏs, i, f., = Τύρος (Heb. ).
Lit., Tyre, a famous maritime and commercial city of the Phœnicians, especially celebrated for its purple, now the ruins of Soor, ; ; ; ; ; ; (4, 12), 7; ; Cv. M. 3, 539; 15, 288.—Hence, Tўrĭus, a, um, adj.
Of or belonging to Tyre, Tyrian: purpura,: murex,; : fucus,: colores,; : vestes,: chlamys,: merces,: puella,i. e. Europa,; also called Tyria paelex,; cf. taurus (that carried her),: Tyria maria in proverbium deductum est, quod Tyro oriundi Poeni adeo potentes maris fuerunt, ut omnibus mortalibus navigatio esset periculosa. Afranius in Epistula: hunc in servum autem maria Tyria conciet, Müll.—
Poet., for Theban (because Thebes was founded by the Phœnician, Cadmus): montes,in the neighborhood of Thebes,; : agri,: ductor,i. e. Eteocles,: exsul,i. e. Polynices,: plectrum,i. e. of Amphion,; cf. chelys,.—
Carthaginian: arces,: virgines,: urbs,: doli,: patres,: ductor,i. e. Hannibal,; cf. miles,the army of Hannibal,.—
Purple, of a purple color: torus,: sinus,: vestes,: palla,: subtemen,: amictus, Ov A. A. 2, 297: cocco tinctum Tyrio,.—Subst.: Tў-rĭum, i, n., a purple color: Tyria atque conchylia et omnis alios colores,; .—Plur subst.: Tўrĭi, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of Tyre, the Tyrians, ; ; ; —Poet., transf. (cf. supra), for Thebans, ; ; .—For Carthaginians, ; ; —
Transf., poet., purple, ; .
